name: action-bar
title: ActionBar
description: The actions for what is selected — a bar that arrives when rows are chosen and leaves when nothing is. React Aria has no ActionBar, so it is built here out of the two things that do exist: React Aria's Toolbar, which makes the bar one tab stop, and the sheet's floating surface, which the popover, the sheet and the toast already share.

files.content:
import { Toolbar as AriaToolbar } from 'react-aria-components' import type { ToolbarProps as AriaToolbarProps } from 'react-aria-components' import { Button } from '../Button/Button' import { SURFACE } from '../popover' import type { KeyboardEvent as ReactKeyboardEvent, ReactNode, Ref } from 'react' /** * The floating surface, pinned to the bottom of the viewport. * * **The boundary colour is moved by a variant rather than by a second class.** `SURFACE` already carries * `border-border-strong`, and two border-colour utilities on one element are decided by the order * Tailwind happens to emit them in, not by the order they are written here — the same trap that made * `Toolbar` grow its own class list instead of wearing this one. `data-[emphasized]:` compiles to an * attribute selector, which outranks the plain utility whatever the order is, so exactly one of the two * colours can ever win. */ const BAR = [ SURFACE, 'fixed inset-x-4 bottom-[calc(1rem+env(safe-area-inset-bottom,0px))] z-40', 'mx-auto flex max-w-3xl p-2', 'data-[emphasized]:border-primary', ].join(' ') const TOOLBAR = 'flex w-full items-center gap-4' const COUNT = 'truncate text-[13px] tabular-nums' const ACTIONS = 'ms-auto flex shrink-0 items-center gap-2' export interface ActionBarProps extends Omit< AriaToolbarProps, 'className' | 'children' | 'orientation' | 'aria-label' | 'ref' > { /** React 19 passes `ref` as an ordinary prop, so no `forwardRef` wrapper. */ ref?: Ref /** * How many items are selected. `0` hides the bar; `'all'` says every one of them is, which is a * different sentence from a large number. * @default 0 */ selectedItemCount?: number | 'all' /** * Called when the clear button is pressed, or when Escape is pressed while the bar has focus. * React Aria reports; it does not clear — the selection belongs to the collection, not to the bar. */ onClearSelection?: () => void /** * Whether the bar is the live one: it takes the accent on its boundary and on its count instead of * the quiet hairline. See the note on the component for what this deliberately does not do. * @default false */ isEmphasized?: boolean /** * The bar's accessible name. It is a toolbar, so it needs one; this says what the bar is about rather * than what is in it. * @default 'Selection actions' */ 'aria-label'?: AriaToolbarProps['aria-label'] className?: string /** The actions themselves — `Button`s, one per thing that can be done to the selection. */ children?: ReactNode } /** * The actions for what is selected — a bar that arrives when rows are chosen and goes away when * nothing is. * * ```tsx * const [selected, setSelected] = useState(new Set()) * * * … *
* * setSelected(new Set())} * > * * * * ``` * * **React Aria has no `ActionBar`, so this is one component built out of two things that do exist**: * React Aria's `Toolbar`, which is what makes the bar **one tab stop** with the arrow keys walking it, * and the sheet's floating surface, which the popover, the sheet and the toast already share. The * reference — React Spectrum S2's `ActionBar` — is a `div` with a `FocusScope`, an entry animation and a * `role="group"` inside it; the semantics here come from the toolbar instead, which is a stronger version * of the same promise: the whole bar is reached in one press of Tab rather than one per action. * * ### The count is the bar's, the selection is not * * `selectedItemCount` and `onClearSelection` are React Spectrum's own pair, and they are what a design * system can honestly publish: **the bar does not own the selection, it reflects it.** The collection * does — React Aria's `Table`, `GridList` and `Tree` all report selection through `onSelectionChange` — * and a bar that kept its own copy would be a second source of truth for the same fact. The same call * `TagGroup`'s `onRemove` makes: a control that *reports* is not a control that *acts*, and a story that * wires it up has to prove the selection is actually gone rather than that a callback fired. * * `0` renders nothing at all rather than an invisible bar — nothing is selected, so there is nothing to * act on, and its controls do not sit in the tab order waiting to be found. * * ### Escape leaves selection mode, and only from inside the bar * * React Spectrum scopes that key to the bar's own element, and so does this: Escape clears while focus * is within the bar, which is where a keyboard user is once they have acted on a row. It does not clear * while focus is out on the page, because a key that empties a selection the reader cannot see the * source of is a key that throws work away. * * **It is also the key React Aria's collections already answer.** `useSelectableCollection` defaults * `escapeKeyBehavior` to `'clearSelection'`, so a `Table` or a `GridList` clears its own selection on * Escape with the bar nowhere near it. The bar is not inventing a key, it is saying the same thing in * the second place a keyboard user ends up. * * ### `isEmphasized` means the accent boundary, not a repaint of everything inside * * S2's emphasized bar flips to a high-contrast container and asks every button inside it to render in a * static colour — "the container decides how its controls look", which does not exist in this system, * where every control sets its own `--btn` and states derive from it. Ported literally it would put a * ghost button's accent label on an accent fill and read as nothing at all. So emphasis here is the * accent on the bar's own boundary and its count: it says which bar is the live one without taking a * single decision away from the controls inside it. * * ### What is deliberately not here * * - **No `scrollRef`, and none of the container arithmetic that goes with it.** In Spectrum it exists so * the bar can be positioned inside a collection's own scroll container and offset by its scrollbar * width. This library's collections are ordinary elements the caller composes, so the bar is fixed to * the viewport and there is no scrollbar to measure. It floats over the page, so a page whose last row * must stay reachable wants a little bottom padding of its own. * - **No exit animation.** The entry is the shared mount animation in `styles.css`, keyed on * `data-slot="action-bar"`, the same one every panel gets. The exit is a hook React Aria keeps private * (`useExitAnimation`), and holding a stale bar mounted to fade it out would be a state machine for * 160ms of polish. * - **The two sentences are English**, like `TagGroup`'s "Remove" and `Toast`'s "Dismiss": the count is * the one string that has to agree with `selectedItemCount`, so it is the component's rather than the * caller's. */ export function ActionBar({ ref, selectedItemCount = 0, onClearSelection, isEmphasized = false, 'aria-label': ariaLabel = 'Selection actions', className, children, ...props }: ActionBarProps) { // Nothing is selected, so the bar is not there at all — see the note above. Everything below is the // bar at rest, which is why this is the first line and not a class on the element. if (selectedItemCount === 0) { return null } return (
) => { if (event.key === 'Escape') { onClearSelection?.() } }} className={[BAR, className].filter(Boolean).join(' ')} >
{/* The label is the button's: an icon-only control with no name is a square. The icon's own `size-4` is what makes it a glyph rather than the 8px cap height of an 11px label — an icon-only control has no label for a cap to track. See `Button.Icon`. */} {/* A live region, so choosing a row is answered out loud — the bar appearing is otherwise a purely visual event, and the count is the page's only statement of what is selected. */} {selectedItemCount === 'all' ? 'All selected' : `${selectedItemCount} selected`}
{children}
) }

import type { ReactNode } from 'react' import { Button as AriaButton } from 'react-aria-components' import type { ButtonProps as AriaButtonProps } from 'react-aria-components' export interface ButtonIconProps { /** * The icon markup, typically an inline `svg]:block [&>svg]:shrink-0', // The default, and only for an icon that did not name its own size — see the note above. '[&>svg:not([class*=size-])]:h-[1cap]', '[&>svg:not([class*=size-])]:w-auto', ].join(' ')} > {children} ) } /** * Layout slot for a `Button` label. Use it as `Button.Text`. Truncates rather * than wrapping so a long label cannot change the control's height. * * Exported as `ButtonText` only so tooling can resolve it; consume the * compound form `Button.Text`. */ export function ButtonText({ children }: ButtonTextProps) { return ( {children} ) } /** * The indeterminate indicator shown while `isPending`. Hand-rolled rather than * React Aria's `ProgressBar`, which renders a `
` — not phrasing content, * so it cannot legally sit inside a `

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-select-menu`, shared by everything that opens over the page: `Menu` now, and
 * `Select` and `ComboBox` when they converge onto it. The same split as `field.ts` — the surface is
 * the thing that must not drift, and the slots are still defined per component so Storybook
 * documents them under the right name.
 *
 * The shadow is the one literal colour in this file: it is a **shadow**, not a surface, and every
 * attempt to derive one from a token produces a haze rather than a shadow. It is `rgba(0,0,0,.7)`
 * because a shadow has to darken in both themes, exactly as the modal's scrim does.
 */
export const SURFACE = [
  'border border-border-strong bg-card rounded-xl',
  'shadow-[0_12px_32px_rgba(0,0,0,.7)]',
  // **A transparent outline at rest, never `outline-none`.** The property is shared —
  // `outline-none` writes `--tw-outline-style`, which every `outline-<width>` reads
  // back — so a ring written beside it can never draw. `Popover` is the part here that
  // takes real focus (a popover with no focusable child is focusable itself).
  'outline-1 -outline-offset-2 outline-transparent',
].join(' ')

/**
 * A popover that holds a single scrolling list: **at least as wide as the control it came from, and
 * wider when an option needs it.**
 *
 * `min-w`, not `w`. A trigger is sized for its own label — a `Select` says "Frankfurt", a `Menu` button
 * says "Actions" — and a panel sized to exactly that cuts off the one option longer than the control,
 * which is usually the option the reader opened the menu to find. Growing to fit the content is what a
 * native popup does, and `w-(--trigger-width)` was the only rule here that could not.
 *
 * The `max-w` is the guard that growth needs: it is the window minus the same 1rem gutter the modal's
 * overlay keeps, so a label long enough to run off the page truncates instead. `min-width` outranks
 * `max-width` in CSS, so a trigger already wider than that cap (a full-width field on a phone) still
 * gets its own width and is never squashed. React Aria writes `--trigger-width` as an inline custom
 * property and no width of its own, so this class is what decides.
 */
export const POPOVER = `flex min-w-(--trigger-width) max-w-[calc(100vw-2rem)] flex-col overflow-clip ${SURFACE}`

/** The list inside it. `max-h` so a long list scrolls rather than running off the page. */
export const LIST =
  'max-h-[264px] overflow-auto overscroll-contain p-0 outline-none'

/**
 * The sheet's `.ds-select-option`: 13px at 75%, with the accent reserved for the choice.
 *
 * Hover and focus land on the same treatment on purpose. A menu is walked with the arrow keys as
 * much as with a pointer, so the row the keyboard has reached and the row the pointer is over
 * should not look like two different kinds of thing.
 */
export const ITEM = [
  'relative flex items-center justify-between gap-3',
  'px-3.5 py-[11px] text-[13px] text-foreground/75',
  'cursor-pointer select-none',
  'data-[hovered]:bg-foreground/7 data-[hovered]:text-foreground',
  'data-[pressed]:bg-foreground/12',
  'data-[focus-visible]:outline-none data-[focus-visible]:bg-foreground/7 data-[focus-visible]:text-foreground',
  'data-[selected]:text-primary',
  'data-[disabled]:cursor-not-allowed data-[disabled]:text-foreground/35',
].join(' ')

/** One item's text, which truncates rather than wrapping a menu wider than its trigger. */
export const ITEM_LABEL = 'truncate'

/** A run of items, announced as a group. */
export const SECTION = 'flex flex-col'

/** The sheet's `.ds-select-group-label`. */
export const SECTION_TITLE = [
  'px-3.5 pt-[9px] pb-1',
  'text-[11px] uppercase tracking-[0.08em] text-foreground/45',
].join(' ')

/** The sheet's `.ds-div-hair`, inset so it reads as a break in the list rather than a table edge. */
export const SEPARATOR = 'my-1 h-px shrink-0 bg-border'

/** A search box above the list sits behind the menu's own hairline, so it reads as part of the surface. */
export const SEARCH = 'border-b border-border-strong p-2'

/**
 * A submenu's caret. A row with a submenu says so — `data-has-submenu` is React Aria's — and an
 * affordance nobody can see is not an affordance.
 */
export const SUBMENU_CARET = [
  'shrink-0 text-foreground/45',
  'motion-safe:transition-[rotate] motion-safe:duration-(--duration-fast) ease-pulse',
  'data-[open]:rotate-90',
].join(' ')

docs:
The actions for what is selected — a bar that arrives when rows are chosen and leaves when nothing is. React Aria has no `ActionBar`, so it is built here out of the two things that do exist: React Aria's `Toolbar`, which makes the bar one tab stop, and the sheet's floating surface, which the popover, the sheet and the toast already share. ```tsx const [selected, setSelected] = useState(new Set(['fra1', 'iad1'])) …
setSelected(new Set())} > ``` | Prop | Type | Notes | | ------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | `selectedItemCount` | `number \| 'all'` | `0` renders nothing; `'all'` renders "All selected" | | `onClearSelection` | `() => void` | The clear button, and Escape while the bar has focus | | `isEmphasized` | `boolean` | The accent on the bar's boundary and its count, on by default off | | `aria-label` | `string` | Names the toolbar. Defaults to "Selection actions" | | `className` | `string` | Appended to the surface's own list | | `children` | `ReactNode` | The actions — `Button`s, one per thing that can be done to them | **It is a `role="toolbar"` with a name**, not a `div` with buttons in it, and that is the whole of what React Aria adds: the bar is **one tab stop** and the arrow keys walk it, so four actions cost a keyboard user one press of Tab rather than four. The name is a prop rather than a fixed string because a page can have more than one bar — a table's and a chart's — and "Selection actions" twice tells a screen reader nothing about which is which. **It is not `Toolbar` with a different class list.** `Toolbar` is `flex items-center gap-1` on a `rounded-md` surface with a `p-1` inset; this is a much larger bar on a `rounded-xl` floating panel. Appending one class list to the other would leave two radii, two paddings and two sets of gaps on one element, and which of each wins is decided by the order Tailwind emits them rather than the order they are written — so the two components share the primitive and not the recipe. ### The count is the bar's, the selection is not `selectedItemCount` and `onClearSelection` are React Spectrum's own pair, and they are what a design system can honestly publish: **the bar reflects a selection, it does not own one.** The collection owns it — React Aria's `Table`, `GridList` and `Tree` all report theirs through `onSelectionChange` — and a bar holding its own copy would be a second source of truth for the same fact, and the one that goes stale first. That makes `onClearSelection` a **request**, exactly as `TagGroup`'s `onRemove` is: it says what the user asked for and leaves the collection to do it. The consequence is a testing rule rather than a naming one — clearing is only proven by the rows being unchecked, never by the callback having been called, which is the mistake `TagGroup` already made once. `ActionBar.browser.test.tsx` asserts both halves. `'all'` is in the union because "412 selected" and "everything selected" are different facts about a filter, and only the caller knows which one it has — a table that has selected every row _of what matches_ is not a table with 412 rows chosen, and the wording should not pretend otherwise. The count is a `role="status"` live region. The bar appearing is otherwise a purely visual event: without it, a keyboard user who has just chosen a row is told nothing at all. ### Escape leaves selection mode, and only from inside the bar React Spectrum scopes that key to the bar's own element and so does this, for a reason worth stating: the selection belongs to a table the reader may be scrolled away from, so a key that empties it from anywhere on the page throws work away with no visible source. Inside the bar, Escape is the way out of selection mode — it is the same contract the reference has. **And it is the key React Aria's own collections already answer.** `useSelectableCollection` defaults `escapeKeyBehavior` to `'clearSelection'`, so a table or a grid list clears its own selection on Escape with the bar nowhere near it — measured here rather than read off: a click on a row followed by Escape empties the selection with focus still on the row. The bar is therefore not inventing a key; it is saying the same thing in the second place a keyboard user ends up. That is also why the browser test contrasts the bar with a page _button_ rather than with the table: a table would have answered on its own, and the test would have proven React Aria's behaviour while claiming the bar's. ### `isEmphasized` is the accent boundary, not a repaint of everything inside S2's emphasized bar flips to a high-contrast container and asks every button inside it to render in a static colour — "the container decides how its controls look". That mechanism does not exist in this system: every control sets its own `--btn` and derives its hover, pressed and disabled states from it, so a container that repainted its children would leave a ghost button's accent label on an accent fill and read as nothing at all. Emphasis here is therefore the accent on the bar's **own** boundary and count: it says which bar is the live one without taking a single decision away from the controls in it. The class is a `data-[emphasized]:` variant rather than a second `border-*` utility, and that is not cosmetic. The surface already declares `border-border-strong`; two border-colour utilities on one element resolve by the order Tailwind emits them in the compiled stylesheet, so a component that looks right in the source can render in the wrong colour and nothing in the file will show it. The attribute selector outranks the plain utility whatever the order. The `Emphasized` story compares the bar's boundary with the accent **as painted on a probe element in the same story**, so the assertion holds in either theme and fails the moment the variant stops outranking the surface. ### What is deliberately not here - **No `scrollRef`, and none of the container arithmetic that goes with it.** In Spectrum it positions the bar inside a collection's own scroll container and offsets it by that container's scrollbar width — and returns an `actionBarHeight` so the collection can reserve room for it. This library's collections are ordinary elements the caller composes, so there is no such container to measure. The bar is `fixed` to the viewport, which is where a bar over a page wants to be; a page whose last row must stay clickable wants a little bottom padding of its own. - **No exit animation.** The entry is the shared mount animation in `styles.css`, keyed on `data-slot="action-bar"` — the same one every panel gets — and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion` like the rest. The exit has no hook to hang off: `useExitAnimation` is private to React Spectrum, and holding a bar with nothing selected mounted for 160ms to fade it out would be a state machine for polish. - **The two sentences are English**, like `TagGroup`'s "Remove" and `Toast`'s "Dismiss". The count is the one string that has to agree with `selectedItemCount`, so it stays the component's; a system that needs another language needs it in the other three places too. ### Where the tests are, and why they are split The states are stories: `Hidden` is the control for the bar existing at all, `AllSelected` is the `'all'` wording, `Emphasized` is the variant winning, and `Keyboard` is the arrow keys walking the bar and staying inside it. **`Default` carries no `play` at all**, because a `play` runs when a story is _viewed_: one that chose rows and then cleared them would be a machine working the same table the reader opened, and it would leave them on a page with no bar to try. What that story demonstrates is covered in `ActionBar.browser.test.tsx`, where nothing runs unless it is asked to — choosing a row brings the bar up with the count that row implies, the header's select-all reads "All selected", clearing is proven by the rows and not by the request, and Escape clears from inside the bar while leaving the page outside it alone. The arrangement, and the reason for it, is the one `Form.browser.test.tsx` records.
